::: {.callout-note title="Independent enrichment pathway"}
The Waterloo Engineering Track is a locally developed TEJ enrichment pathway. It is not created, approved, or endorsed by the University of Waterloo, it does not reproduce a Waterloo course, and it does not guarantee admission or university credit. The name identifies the preparation goal. The mathematical and engineering habits are intended to be useful for many first- and second-year engineering pathways.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Planning status"}
This is a work-in-progress curriculum plan. Existing linked TEJ lessons and assignments may be used now. WET-coded handouts, answer keys, and the thermal-process capstone must be developed, safety-checked, accessibility-reviewed, and classroom-tested before release.
:::

## Purpose

The student completes the regular TEJ sequence, laboratories, safety requirements, and projects. Track work extends selected TEJ activities with more algebra, systems of equations, conservation laws, energy balances, measurement analysis, programming, modelling, optimization, and technical communication.

The track is not a separate chemical-engineering course and should not become a collection of disconnected university problems. Every extension begins with a real TEJ circuit, measurement, program, computer system, sensor, actuator, or controller. Applications then connect the same mathematics to electrical, computer, mechanical, mechatronics, systems, chemical, civil, environmental, and related engineering fields.

The pathway is designed around four recurring questions:

1. What is the system boundary?
2. What quantities enter, leave, accumulate, or are transformed?
3. What equations and assumptions represent the system?
4. Do calculated, simulated, and measured results agree closely enough to support the conclusion?

## Relationship to Waterloo engineering

Waterloo's current first-year examples vary by program, but the common preparation pattern is mathematics, physical science, computation, design, laboratories, and communication. Electrical Engineering emphasizes calculus, linear algebra, programming, circuits, logic, and physics. Mechanical Engineering emphasizes mathematics, mechanics, chemistry, materials, electrical engineering, and design. Mechatronics combines mathematics, computation, circuits, statics, materials, and algorithms. Systems Design emphasizes mathematics, computation, modelling, design, communication, and human or ecological systems. Chemical Engineering combines mathematics, chemistry, programming, engineering concepts, laboratories, and design.

Current program descriptions are available from Waterloo for [Electrical Engineering](https://uwaterloo.ca/future-students/programs/electrical-engineering), [Mechanical Engineering](https://uwaterloo.ca/future-students/programs/mechanical-engineering), [Mechatronics Engineering](https://uwaterloo.ca/engineering/future-students/mechatronics-engineering), [Systems Design Engineering](https://uwaterloo.ca/future-students/programs/systems-design-engineering), and [Chemical Engineering](https://uwaterloo.ca/future-students/programs/chemical-engineering). Course names and sequences can change; these links are context, not track requirements.

## Intended learning outcomes

By the end of the pathway, the student should be able to:

1. define variables, units, directions, sign conventions, assumptions, and a system boundary before calculating;
2. use dimensional analysis, engineering notation, significant figures, estimation, and a complete GUESS solution;
3. derive equations from circuit and system diagrams instead of selecting formulas by appearance;
4. solve and verify two- and three-variable linear systems by substitution, elimination, and matrix or software methods;
5. apply conservation of charge, current, voltage, power, energy, and material to appropriate models;
6. collect repeatable data, construct calibration models, quantify error, and distinguish interpolation from unsupported extrapolation;
7. implement a discrete-time model in a spreadsheet or program and compare its prediction with measurements;
8. compare design alternatives using constraints, efficiency, sensitivity, cost, safety, and uncertainty;
9. design, build, program, test, revise, and communicate a small instrumented engineering system.

## Pathway structure

The suggested pathway adds approximately 35 to 50 hours across a full TEJ course. Most work replaces a simpler practice set or adds one challenge section; it should not become an unmanageable second course. Chapters WET01 through WET06 establish the minimum analytical core. Later chapters may be selected to match the student's interests and available equipment.

## Chapter specifications

### WET00 Engineering baseline and notebook

The track begins with a short diagnostic rather than a mark. The student demonstrates fraction and decimal operations, equation rearrangement, graph interpretation, unit conversions, calculator use, estimation, and a short technical explanation. The result determines which skills require review.

The engineering notebook standard requires a dated problem statement, system diagram, givens, unknowns, assumptions, equations before substitution, units carried through the work, full calculator result, rounded answer, reasonableness check, and revision record. Safety decisions and failed tests remain part of the record.

### WET01 Quantities, units, and scale

Complete [Number Systems, Measurement, Units, and Calculator Skills](../01-number-systems/index.qmd), then extend the work to compound units such as coulombs per second, joules per second, watt-hours, kilograms per second, litres per minute, joules per kilogram-degree Celsius, revolutions per minute, radians per second, and dollars per kilowatt-hour.

The student should convert units by multiplying by identities, not by moving decimals without explanation. Estimation precedes calculator work. Final answers must state whether the magnitude is physically plausible.

### WET02 Algebraic electrical models

Complete [Charge, Voltage, and Current](../02-basic-electronics/01-charge-voltage-current.qmd), [Closed, Open, and Short Circuits](../02-basic-electronics/02-circuits-opens-shorts.qmd), and [Ohm's Law](../02-basic-electronics/03-ohms-law.qmd).

Track problems require the student to derive and rearrange relationships, identify impossible values, state operating limits, and compare symbolic predictions with simulation. Problems should include design choices rather than only asking for a missing number.

### WET03 Conservation in series and parallel networks

Use the regular H09 and H10 circuit sequence. The extension emphasizes why the current, voltage, resistance, and power rules follow from circuit structure. Each solution includes at least two independent checks.

The student should be able to demonstrate:

$$I_T=I_1=I_2 \quad \text{for one series path}$$

$$V_T=V_1=V_2 \quad \text{for parallel branches across the same nodes}$$

$$P_T=\sum P_k$$

The power equation is used as a conservation check after the circuit has been solved.

### WET04 Coupled equations, KCL, and KVL

This chapter is the central systems-of-equations experience. Grob Chapter 9 explicitly progresses from KCL and KVL to branch-current, node-voltage, and mesh-current methods. The student first solves a two-source network using elimination, then expresses the same equations in matrix form, and finally uses software to verify the result. [[1, Ch. 9]](../../references.qmd#ref-grob2016)

The solution must include a labelled schematic, assumed directions, independent node and loop equations, the algebraic solution, substitution back into the original equations, a KCL residual, a KVL residual, and a power balance. A negative current is interpreted as evidence that the actual direction is opposite to the assumed reference, not as a failed calculation.

### WET05 Equivalent models and optimization

Thevenin and Norton equivalents reduce a network to a useful model at two terminals. The student varies a load, graphs delivered power, identifies a maximum, and then explains why maximum power is not always the same design objective as maximum efficiency, minimum cost, lowest temperature, or longest battery life.

This chapter introduces engineering optimization without requiring calculus. A valid recommendation must name the objective, constraints, variables, feasible alternatives, evidence, and trade-offs.

### WET06 Power and energy balances

Complete [Power and Energy](../02-basic-electronics/04-power-energy.qmd), then apply a conserved-quantity balance:

$$\text{input}-\text{output}=\text{accumulation}$$

For a material species that can be produced or consumed, the more general form also includes generation and consumption terms. For total energy, energy may cross the boundary or change form, but it is conserved.

For an electrical load:

$$P=VI \qquad E_{\mathrm{in}}=VIt$$

For a supervised low-voltage water-heating investigation:

$$E_{\mathrm{water}}=mc\Delta T$$

$$E_{\mathrm{in}}=E_{\mathrm{stored}}+E_{\mathrm{loss}}$$

$$\eta=\frac{E_{\mathrm{useful}}}{E_{\mathrm{in}}}\times100\%$$

The introductory calculation treats water as a closed batch and calculates an observed loss. The advanced investigation uses two experimental runs to estimate an effective heat capacity $C_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and a heat-loss coefficient $K$:

$$\overline V_j\overline I_jt_j=C_{\mathrm{eff}}\Delta T_j+K(T_{\mathrm{avg},j}-T_{\mathrm{room},j})t_j$$

Two runs produce two linear equations. A third run tests the model. Çengel Chapters 3, 5, and 6 provide the teacher background for energy analysis, closed systems, and control volumes; the student activity remains original, low-voltage, and appropriate for TEJ. [[27, Chs. 3, 5-6]](../../references.qmd#ref-cengel2008)

::: {.callout-important title="Thermal-project safety boundary"}
Use only teacher-approved protected low-voltage equipment. Students do not construct or probe mains circuits. Keep liquids isolated from exposed electronics, include temperature and current limits, provide secondary containment, and define a safe shutdown state before testing.
:::

### WET07 Measurement, calibration, and uncertainty

Use H05 and BB06 to compare calculated, simulated, and measured values. Calibrate one sensor or actuator using repeated measurements. The student produces a scatter plot, fitted relationship, residual table, stated valid range, and discussion of uncertainty.

The objective is not to force every data set to be linear. The student must explain whether the model is suitable, where interpolation is defensible, and why extrapolation beyond the measured range may be unsafe.

### WET08 Transient and discrete-time systems

RC and LR circuits provide a TEJ route into changing systems. The student measures or simulates a transient, identifies a time constant, and compares observations with a model. A spreadsheet or program then advances the model one time step at a time.

For the thermal process, an accessible no-calculus model is:

$$T_{n+1}=T_n+\frac{P_{\mathrm{in}}-K(T_n-T_{\mathrm{room}})}{C_{\mathrm{eff}}}\Delta t$$

The student changes the time step and explains why a numerical model can become inaccurate or unstable. Differential equations may be named as the later university language for the same idea, but they are not required to complete the track.

### WET09 Logic, algorithms, and state

Complete the [Digital Logic and Stable Inputs](../03-digital-logic-inputs/index.qmd) sequence and the appropriate Programming and Microcontroller modules. Three-input truth tables must count in binary order from $000$ to $111$, with a separate column for each output.

The programming extension implements one previously solved model. Suitable programs include a GUESS calculator with unit checks, a two- or three-equation solver, an RC simulator, a thermal time-step model, or a calibration tool. The student supplies tests, explains invalid-input handling, and compares program output with one hand calculation.

### WET10 Electromechanical systems

Use magnetism, electromagnetism, switching, motors, protection, and motion control to connect electrical input to mechanical output. The minimum mathematical set is:

$$P_{\mathrm{electrical}}=VI$$

$$P_{\mathrm{mechanical}}=\tau\omega$$

$$\eta=\frac{P_{\mathrm{mechanical}}}{P_{\mathrm{electrical}}}$$

The student characterizes one approved actuator or pump across several operating points and explains why speed, torque, flow, current, temperature, and efficiency cannot all be optimized independently.

### WET11 Feedback, models, and design decisions

Complete the [Control Systems and CNC](../05-control-systems/index.qmd) comparison sequence. Use the same process model and disturbance when comparing open loop, on-off control, hysteresis, proportional control, and PI or PID control. Record rise time, overshoot, settling behaviour, steady-state error, saturation, and failure response.

Calculus is not required. The student should understand the operational meaning of accumulated error and rate of change, use graphs accurately, and explain how changing a parameter affects the complete system.

### WET12 Integrated engineering project

The recommended project is an **instrumented low-voltage thermal process controller**. It connects TEJ circuits, sensors, microcontrollers, programming, energy, data, safety, and control while providing useful preparation across engineering disciplines.

The student may propose a different project when it preserves the same mathematical and validation requirements. Suitable alternatives include a motor or pump test stand, battery discharge and thermal monitor, environmental chamber model, controlled fan-and-temperature system, tank-level simulator, or instrumented renewable-energy demonstrator.

## Capstone gates

| Gate | Approval evidence |
|---|---|
| 1. Need and system boundary | stakeholder or use case, measurable need, inputs, outputs, disturbances and exclusions |
| 2. Safety and feasibility | low-voltage boundary, hazards, limits, fault response, available equipment and teacher approval |
| 3. Mathematical model | variables, units, assumptions, governing equations, expected range and hand-worked example |
| 4. Electrical design | readable schematic, component ratings, protection, power budget and interface limits |
| 5. Experimental plan | controlled variables, calibration, sampling plan, uncertainty and success criteria |
| 6. Prototype or simulation | functional implementation, versioned code and initial data |
| 7. Validation | predicted-versus-measured comparison, residuals, limitations and model revision |
| 8. Communication | concise report, graphs, annotated evidence, references, demonstration and reflection |

## Assessment model

Track work should be assessed as engineering evidence rather than extra arithmetic. The recommended weighting within each major task is:

| Category | Weight | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Model formulation | 25% | boundary, variables, assumptions, diagram and equations |
| Mathematical execution | 20% | algebra, units, precision, software use and verification |
| Design and safety | 20% | ratings, constraints, protection, feasible choices and fault response |
| Experiment and validation | 20% | calibration, repeatability, comparison, uncertainty and revision |
| Communication | 15% | organized notebook, graphs, citations, explanation and conclusion |

A polished answer with an unjustified model should not receive a high track result. A student who discovers and explains why a model failed may demonstrate stronger engineering judgement than a student whose numbers happen to agree.

## Discipline connections

| Engineering direction | Strongest track connections |
|---|---|
| Electrical and Computer | circuits, KCL/KVL, equivalent networks, power, logic, programming, embedded systems and control |
| Mechanical and Mechatronics | energy conversion, sensors, actuators, torque, motion, thermal behaviour, programming and control |
| Systems Design | boundaries, requirements, models, feedback, trade-offs, optimization, uncertainty and communication |
| Chemical and Biological | conservation laws, energy balances, transient models, sensors, process data and control |
| Civil and Environmental | measurement, flow and energy analogies, structures or networks, data models, optimization and sustainability |
| Management and Industrial | process mapping, constraints, data, efficiency, optimization, cost and decision records |

## Textbook chapter map

The textbooks are teacher references. Public track materials must use original explanations, diagrams, values, and questions. Do not copy or republish textbook pages or problem sets.

### Grob's Basic Electronics, 12th edition

| Chapters used | Track use |
|---|---|
| Ch. 0, Introduction to Powers of 10 | engineering notation, metric prefixes and calculator fluency |
| Ch. 1, Electricity | charge, current, voltage, power, energy and physical foundations |
| Ch. 3, Ohm's Law | algebraic electrical models |
| Chs. 4-6, Series, Parallel, and Series-Parallel Circuits | network structure and conservation checks |
| Ch. 7, Voltage Dividers and Current Dividers | proportional models and loading |
| Ch. 8, Analog and Digital Multimeters | measurement practice |
| Ch. 9, Kirchhoff's Laws | KCL, KVL, branch currents, node voltage, mesh current and simultaneous equations |
| Ch. 10, Network Theorems | equivalent models and maximum-power investigations |
| Ch. 12, Batteries | stored energy, capacity and source behaviour |
| Chs. 13-14, Magnetism and Electromagnetism | electromechanical systems |
| Chs. 16, 18-22 | capacitance, inductance, transients and time constants |
| Chs. 27-30 and 33 | optional device, switching, sensor-interface and op-amp extensions |

Grob remains the primary electronics sequencing source. [[1]](../../references.qmd#ref-grob2016)

### Çengel, Introduction to Thermodynamics and Heat Transfer, 2nd edition

| Chapters used | Teacher use in the track |
|---|---|
| Ch. 1, Introduction and Overview | units, systematic problem solving, modelling and systems of equations |
| Ch. 3, Energy, Energy Transfer, and General Energy Analysis | energy forms, balances, conversion and efficiency |
| Ch. 5, Energy Analysis of Closed Systems | batch thermal system background |
| Ch. 6, Mass and Energy Analysis of Control Volumes | optional flow-system extension |
| Ch. 9, Mechanisms of Heat Transfer | conduction, convection and radiation vocabulary |
| Ch. 11, Transient Heat Conduction | advanced interpretation of time-dependent heating and cooling |

This is a restricted teacher reference. Student materials use a deliberately smaller high-school model. [[27]](../../references.qmd#ref-cengel2008)

### Chapra and Canale, Numerical Methods for Engineers, 6th edition

| Chapters used | Teacher use in the track |
|---|---|
| Ch. 1, Mathematical Modeling and Engineering Problem Solving | conservation-law models across engineering disciplines |
| Ch. 2, Programming and Software | structured computational implementation |
| Chs. 3-4, Error Analysis | significant figures, accuracy, precision, uncertainty and error propagation |
| Chs. 5-6, Roots of Equations | graphical solutions, iteration and convergence extensions |
| Chs. 9-12, Linear Algebraic Equations | elimination, matrices, software verification and cross-discipline cases |
| Chs. 13-16, Optimization | design variables, objectives, constraints and discipline examples |
| Chs. 17 and 20, Curve Fitting and Case Studies | regression and experimental data |
| Chs. 25 and 28, Ordinary Differential Equations and Case Studies | teacher background for discrete transient models |

Chapter 12 is particularly useful as a teacher reference because it places reactor, truss, resistor-circuit, and spring-mass examples beside one another, showing that linear systems are shared engineering tools. Chapter 16 similarly compares tank, wastewater, circuit, and mechanical optimization cases. Track assignments remain original and use high-school mathematics. [[28]](../../references.qmd#ref-chapra2010)

## Implementation status

This page defines the intended track and source map. Existing TEJ lessons and linked activities can be used now. WET-coded assignments and the thermal-process capstone still require separate student handouts, answer keys, equipment verification, accessibility review, and classroom piloting before they are labelled published.
